title: Segmented gate: negative retention finger guards the storage junction
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation resolves 'strong on-current vs. tiny off-leakage': split the buried wordline into a long drive segment on the bitline side and a short, independently driven 'retention finger' over the storage-node junction. The finger sits at about -1 V except during the ~20 ns activation, so the drain field and trap-assisted tunnelling at the storage node are borne by a deeply-off segment while the drive segment can use a lower Vt.
why: Attacks Fact 3 (<=13 fA tail, GIDL/TAT dominated): target 10-50x lower tail leakage, stretching refresh from 32-64 ms toward ~1 s and recovering most of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss, at the cost of a second wordline driver per row.

title: Tail-bit eviction table lets the bulk array refresh 16x slower
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: extract the few harmful cells instead of running the whole array at their pace. At final test each die is screened against a 1 s / 85 C retention target; the ~1e-5 of bits that fail are fuse-mapped into a per-bank CAM + SRAM 'tail cache' (~32 kb) that transparently intercepts their reads and writes, with on-die ECC covering variable-retention escapees.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (Fact 3): refresh is set by the 99.999th percentile, not the worst cell, giving 8-16x fewer refresh operations for ~0.3-0.5% die area; idle refresh power drops from 16-33% to a few percent.

title: Deuterium passivation targeted only at the storage-node junction
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: the leakage tail lives at the storage-node junction and its interface traps, so give that one spot a different material property. A self-aligned opening at the storage-node contact admits a deuterium implant plus anneal; Si-D bonds resist hot-carrier and thermal depassivation far better than Si-H (giant isotope effect), so tail traps stay passivated over life and VRT is suppressed.
why: Narrows the retention tail and variable-retention-time population (Fact 3); claim 2-4x longer worst-case retention using only an extra masked implant.

title: Lattice-matched GaP pocket on the storage side kills band-to-band tunnelling
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: the access transistor needs a high bandgap only where it leaks, not where it drives. Selectively grow a lattice-matched GaP pocket (Eg 2.26 eV, ~0.4% mismatch to Si) on just the storage-node side of the recessed channel; band-to-band tunnelling falls roughly exponentially with Eg^1.5 while the Si bitline side keeps full drive.
why: GIDL under negative wordline bias is a dominant tail mechanism (Fact 3): claim ~100x lower GIDL, allowing a shallower negative wordline (smaller pumps, Fact 10) and 4-8x longer refresh.

title: Back-to-back refresh rows hand their wordline charge to each other
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging (in time): refresh is the only DRAM operation whose next row is known in advance, so merge the falling edge of row i with the rising edge of row i+1. A charge-sharing switch between the two local wordline drivers dumps about half of row i's ~3 V wordline charge into row i+1 before the VPP pump tops it up, and bitline precharge charge is likewise recycled across consecutive refreshes in a mat.
why: Attacks refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, Fact 3) and the wordline CV^2 floor (Fact 10): ~30-45% less VPP pump energy per refresh, amplified because charge pumps run at only ~30% efficiency.

title: Wordline bootstrap capacitor doubles as an analog hammer counter
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: make an element already present in every row do a second job. Each local wordline driver gets a tiny MIM capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet on every activation (a switched-capacitor integrator) and is cleared on refresh; when it crosses a comparator threshold the driver flags its two neighbours for targeted refresh, giving exact per-row activation counting without SRAM counter tables.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (Fact 9) forces extra refresh: exact per-row analog counting replaces kilobits of counter SRAM and probabilistic schemes, cutting mitigation refreshes 5-10x with no coverage holes.

title: Access transistor nested inside the capacitor's hollow pillar
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: use the hollow core of the tall cylinder capacitor as the body of a vertical access transistor. An ALD channel lines the upper inner wall and a gate electrode fills the core, so the device gets a 150-300 nm channel length (killing DIBL and short-channel subthreshold leakage) without using any lateral area.
why: Breaks the 'smaller cell vs. longer, less leaky channel' contradiction (Facts 2, 3): ~10x lower subthreshold leakage and a route to 4F2 without a separate transistor tier.

title: Age-tracking sense reference counterweights expected charge decay
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight: oppose the 'weight' of leakage with a counter-force. Because retention failures are overwhelmingly charged-to-discharged, the sense-amplifier reference (reference-cell charge or bitline precharge offset) is stepped down according to the known age of each row since its last restore (derived from the refresh counter), following the measured decay curve, so a partly drained '1' still reads and restores correctly.
why: Extends the usable refresh interval 2-4x (Fact 3) by spending the unused margin on the '0' side; costs a small reference DAC per sense-amp group.

title: Park bitlines at VDD during self-refresh to zero ones' drain bias
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: remove the harmful driving force before it acts. During long idle and self-refresh, bitlines are parked at VDD instead of VDD/2, so the vulnerable charged '1' cells see zero drain-source voltage and essentially no subthreshold loss, while '0' cells, protected by the negative wordline and far from their sense threshold, absorb the larger bias.
why: Removes the subthreshold component of the retention tail in standby (Fact 3): ~2-3x longer self-refresh interval for idle phones and servers at zero area cost.

title: Sort-time electrothermal annealing heals leakage-tail cells individually
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: fix the defect before the part ships. At wafer sort, cells flagged as retention-tail are driven with short high-current pulses through their own and neighbouring access transistors to self-heat the junction region to several hundred C for microseconds, annealing the specific trap responsible, then retested; cells that still fail fall back to row repair.
why: Turns tail cells into normal cells (Fact 3), shrinking repair overhead and permitting longer refresh, while recovering yield, a direct capacity lever.

title: Deliberately weak canary cells trigger refresh per mat only when needed
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: plant a sacrificial early warning. Each mat includes a few canary cells with ~50% of normal capacitance and a slightly leakier junction; a tiny always-on comparator polls them, and the mat is refreshed only when a canary flips, automatically tracking local temperature, voltage, aging and process corner (ECC backs up the rare cell weaker than its canary).
why: Most mats retain far longer than the 64 ms worst case (Fact 3): per-mat demand refresh claims 4-10x fewer refreshes at typical temperatures.

title: Bootstrapped guard node gives the inner switch zero voltage to leak
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality (the electrometer guard trick): put two access transistors in series and drive their middle node from a source follower whose gate is the storage node. In retention the inner transistor sees ~0 V across it and leaks almost nothing, while all leakage from the bitline is absorbed by the actively driven guard node.
why: Subthreshold current scales as (1 - exp(-Vds/kT)), so holding Vds ~ 0 gives ~100x lower leakage (Fact 3): seconds-scale retention for a 3T cell, trading some density for refresh-free cache/HBM tiers.

title: Leak-safe polarity coding; rows with no charged cells skip refresh
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of fighting the direction leakage pushes, store data in the state leakage drives toward. A per-64-bit inversion flag chosen at write time minimises the number of charged cells; rows whose charged-cell count is zero (zeroed pages, sparse or quantised tensors) are flagged and never refreshed, and refresh priority follows charged-cell count.
why: Many rows are mostly zero (freed pages, sparse AI data): claim 30-60% fewer refreshes and lower exposure to the leakage tail (Fact 3).

title: Curvature-rounded, ultra-graded storage junction to flatten peak field
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: replace sharp corners with curves. A hydrogen-anneal silicon-migration step rounds the recess-channel corners at the storage-node edge, and a laser-spike-diffused wide graded junction replaces the abrupt one, cutting the peak lateral field from ~1 MV/cm toward ~0.6 MV/cm, where trap-assisted tunnelling depends exponentially on field.
why: Shrinks the TAT/GIDL tail (Fact 3) ~5-10x with existing tool types; low-cost, incremental.

title: Per-row programmable Vt via charge-trap layer in the wordline stack
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: make a fixed property adjustable. A thin SiN charge-trap layer in the buried-wordline gate stack lets each row's access-transistor Vt be programmed by Fowler-Nordheim pulses at test and retrimmed in the field: leaky rows get ~+200 mV of Vt, strong rows keep low Vt for speed.
why: Compresses the retention distribution so refresh is set by a trimmed tail (Fact 3): 3-5x longer refresh interval without a global speed penalty.

title: Refresh only live sub-row segments using gated local wordlines
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial action: do only as much as needed. Split each row's local wordline into eight sub-row segments with per-segment 'live' bits set by writes and cleared by OS free/zeroing commands; refresh activates only live segments, so refresh energy and bandwidth scale with resident data rather than capacity.
why: Refresh energy (Fact 3) and overfetch (Fact 8): 2-5x lower refresh energy in partially used memories, far finer than bank-level partial-array self-refresh.

title: Flip the stack so memory dies, not logic, touch the cold plate
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: use the vertical heat path instead of fighting it in-plane. In HBM and 3D stacks, place the DRAM dies against the cold plate and route the logic base-die heat out through a separate high-conductivity path (thermal TSV bundles plus a backside spreader), so the memory runs ~20-30 C cooler; cell leakage roughly halves every ~10 C.
why: Refresh rate doubles above 85 C today (Fact 3): 4-8x lower cell leakage lets HBM leave 2x refresh mode, regaining up to 10-20% bandwidth.

title: Resonant LC drivers sweep refresh wordlines adiabatically
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration / resonance: refresh is perfectly periodic and predictable, so drive it with a resonance. Package-level inductors form an LC tank with a bank's refresh wordline and bitline load, so lines rise and fall as sine half-cycles and their energy is recovered rather than dissipated through the ~3 V VPP pump.
why: Attacks the CV^2 floor (Fact 10) and refresh energy (Fact 3): claim 40-60% lower refresh energy without changing the cell.

title: Parametron cells: pumped phase-encoded bits that never need refresh
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: replace static charge with a sustained oscillation. Each cell is a tiny resonator built around a nonlinear (antiferroelectric) varactor, pumped at 2f from a shared plate line; parametric bistability locks it into one of two oscillation phases (0 or pi) that store the bit, and the pump continuously replaces what leakage removes.
why: Eliminates refresh as a concept and makes read non-destructive (Facts 3, 8); risks are resonator size and pump power, reviving Goto's 1954 parametron at nanoscale.

title: Two-threshold margin sensing during refresh learns each row's retention online
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: refresh is pure overhead, so make every refresh also a measurement. Sense amps perform a second, offset sensing pass during refresh; rows whose '1' signal has decayed past a warning threshold are promoted to a faster refresh bin and rows with large margin are demoted to slower bins, building a live per-row retention map that tracks VRT and aging.
why: Replaces worst-case 64 ms with learned bins (Fact 3): 4-8x fewer refreshes, robust to variable-retention cells that defeat one-time test profiling.

title: Compiler-tagged ephemeral memory that is never refreshed
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: let data that will die anyway go unrefreshed. Compilers and AI runtimes place allocations whose lifetime is shorter than guaranteed retention (activations, KV-cache blocks overwritten each step, staging buffers) in an 'ephemeral' region whose rows the controller never refreshes, with a hardware write-timestamp that faults reads of expired data.
why: Much of AI memory traffic is short-lived (Facts 3, 5): claim 30-70% fewer refreshes in accelerator memory and recovered bandwidth, with no device change.

title: Buy retention-reject DRAM and qualify it for cooled datacenters
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: dies binned out for leakage-tail failures at 85 C / 64 ms are not dead, only heat-intolerant. A business buys these rejects, re-screens them at 25-40 C with a 16-32 ms refresh contract, and sells them as qualified modules for immersion- or liquid-cooled racks, with controller firmware enforcing each module's refresh profile.
why: Raises usable supply by recovering a few percent of output from existing fabs with zero new capex; buyers get bits well below 4x contract prices.

title: Run memory at 150-200 K and redesign the access device for it
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: change temperature instead of geometry. Cooling DRAM to ~150-200 K on a shared refrigerant loop cuts thermal leakage by many orders so retention reaches minutes; then exploit it by lowering the access-transistor Vt and shortening its channel for a smaller, faster cell at lower wordline voltage.
why: Refresh practically disappears (Fact 3) and lower Vt enables lower VPP (Fact 10): claim >50% memory energy reduction net of cooling at rack scale.

title: Coulomb-blockade island chain as a leak-proof access channel on quartz
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation, taken to the extreme: segment the access channel into a chain of 1-2 nm nanocrystal islands self-assembled on a quartz or sapphire substrate (no silicon wafer). In the off state the single-electron charging energy (>> kT at room temperature for <2 nm islands) blocks transport exponentially with chain length; the wordline gate lifts the blockade for access.
why: Leakage is set by charging energy rather than doping or bandgap (Fact 3): theoretical off-current far below 1e-21 A for hours of retention; bottom-up assembly avoids EUV (Fact 4).

title: Silicon-carbide 1T1C DRAM with hours-long native retention
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change (bandgap): build 1T1C cells on 4H-SiC wafers (Eg 3.26 eV, intrinsic carrier density ~1e18x lower than Si), where 1990s SiC DRAM test cells already showed hours-to-years room-temperature retention. A buried-channel SiC MOS access device at relaxed 40-90 nm rules serves as a refresh-free capacity tier.
why: Refresh eliminated (Fact 3); SiC boules grow by sublimation, sidestepping Spruce Pine quartz crucibles; existing U.S. SiC wafer capacity improves domestic manufacturability. Density is lower, so it targets capacity/standby tiers.

title: LCD backplanes are already 1T1C DRAM: repurpose glass-panel fabs
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: every LCD/OLED pixel is a thin-film transistor plus storage capacitor refreshed at 1-120 Hz, and LTPO oxide TFTs already hold charge at 1 Hz. Redesign Gen-6/8.5 glass backplanes at ~1 um rules into mm-scale memory tiles with LTPS periphery, stacked in several TFT tiers, refreshed at ~1 Hz instead of every 64 ms.
why: Capital intensity (Fact 4): display capex per m2 is orders of magnitude lower than DRAM capex per m2 and needs no EUV; refresh power becomes negligible (Fact 3). Density (~10-20 Mb/cm2 per tier) and TFT periphery speed limit it to CXL/capacity tiers.

title: Stainless-steel foil substrate doubles as global back gate and heatsink
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: make the substrate do three jobs. Oxide or 2D thin-film access transistors are built on a dielectric-coated stainless-steel foil; the foil itself is a static global back gate biased negative to push every array transistor into deep off-state, while also spreading heat and shielding the array (periphery lives on a separate die).
why: Deep off-state without per-row negative wordline pumps (Facts 3, 7, 10); roll-to-roll foil processing cuts capital per bit and uses abundant U.S. steel.

title: Memory arrays fabricated inside the glass-core package substrate
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: merge memory with a part every accelerator already needs, the package substrate. Glass-core substrates entering production for large AI packages get panel-processed oxide-TFT 1T1C memory layers in their build-up stack directly under the die shadow, connected by fine-pitch vias, so a slow-refresh capacity tier rides beneath each processor without separate dies or TSVs.
why: Data-movement energy (Fact 5) and the HBM TSV tax (Fact 6) for a capacity tier; panel processing cuts capital per bit; ultralow-leakage TFTs allow ~1 Hz refresh (Fact 3).

title: Self-ordered anodic-alumina pores host lithography-free coaxial access transistors
idea: TRIZ #31 Porous materials: anodise an aluminium foil or Al-coated glass panel so it self-organises into hexagonal nanopores at 30-60 nm pitch (~1e10-1e11 per cm2). ALD lines each pore coaxially with bottom electrode, wide-gap oxide channel, gate dielectric and a wrap gate at the top, with the lower pore volume forming the storage capacitor: gate-all-around access at near-4F2 density without EUV.
why: Attacks capital intensity (Fact 4: 5-7 EUV layers) while GAA electrostatics plus wide-gap channels cut leakage (Fact 3); aluminium is abundant and U.S.-produced. Wordline/bitline addressing at pore pitch is the hard part.

title: Hermetic NEMS relay access switch: an air gap is the perfect off-state
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution, inverted: replace the field-effect switch with an electrostatically actuated nano-cantilever relay built on glass and sealed in a vacuum/inert micro-cavity. Open, the gap gives zero channel leakage so retention is set only by capacitor dielectric leakage (minutes to hours); closed, a metal contact gives near-ideal write/read with abrupt switching at low actuation voltage.
why: Eliminates the access-transistor leakage tail entirely (Fact 3) and the 3 V wordline (Fact 10) via abrupt actuation; key risks are contact endurance at 1e12-1e15 cycles and ns-scale switching.

title: Vacuum-nanogap field-emission access transistor on sapphire
idea: TRIZ #39 Inert atmosphere (vacuum): a <50 nm vacuum channel, operable near atmospheric pressure because it is shorter than the mean free path of air, separates a sharp emitter from the storage electrode on a sapphire substrate, with a surrounding gate modulating field emission. With no semiconductor in the channel there is no thermal generation or band-to-band leakage in the off state.
why: Off-state leakage effectively zero (Fact 3), radiation-hard and heat-tolerant, so no high-temperature refresh derating; risks are emitter stability and turn-on voltage (Fact 10).

title: Light is the wordline: photoconductive access switches on glass
idea: TRIZ #32 Changing optical properties: each cell's access switch is a high-dark-resistivity photoconductor (e.g., low-temperature-grown GaAs or amorphous-selenium-class film, >1e12 ohm-cm dark) on transparent glass, opened by a picosecond pulse from a row waveguide. Off leakage is set by dark conductivity, the optical wordline carries no CV2 charge, and wordline coupling disturbs vanish.
why: Removes the ~3 V wordline energy (Fact 10) and hammer coupling (Fact 9) with very low dark leakage for long retention (Fact 3); requires on-panel laser and waveguide integration.

title: Persistent-current superconducting loops on sapphire for cryogenic racks
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: below Tc a superconducting loop's circulating current never decays, so retention is infinite. Patterned NbN or NbTiN nanowire loops on sapphire store a bit as clockwise or counter-clockwise flux, written and read through nanowire cryotrons (nTrons), giving byte-addressable cryogenic memory for superconducting logic and 4 K quantum-control systems.
why: Zero refresh and attojoule switching (Facts 3, 10); a niche (cryogenic computing) where DRAM fails outright, with ~1 um2 cells reachable; cooling cost limits scope.

title: Surface-acoustic-wave wordline gates 2D channels on piezoelectric substrate
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration: on lithium niobate or AlScN-on-sapphire, a GHz surface acoustic wave launched along a row carries a piezoelectric potential that momentarily opens MoS2 access channels as it passes, so the 'wordline' is a travelling wave, not a charged metal line. Between waves the channels sit deeply off with no static gate bias; row latency is transit time (~30 ns per 100 um).
why: Eliminates wordline CV2 and negative-bias pumps (Facts 7, 10) and row-hammer coupling (Fact 9) while keeping off-state leakage minimal (Fact 3); coupling strength is speculative.

title: GaN/AlN tunnel-diode pair self-holds the bit without refresh
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: let the cell maintain itself. On GaN-on-sapphire, two room-temperature GaN/AlN resonant tunnelling diodes are stacked in series with the storage node at their midpoint; their negative-differential-resistance curves intersect at two stable points, so the node self-restores against leakage at pA standby current, accessed through one GaN HEMT.
why: Refresh eliminated (Fact 3) with non-destructive hold; risk is RTD peak-to-valley ratio and standby current per bit (needs <10 pA/bit for 1 Gb under 10 mW).

title: Grow on reusable single-crystal wafers, laser-lift-off the memory film
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: grow single-crystal wide-gap channel layers (GaN, AlGaN or Ga2O3) on sapphire or bulk-oxide growth wafers, bond them to cheap glass panels, and laser-lift-off the film as in micro-LED and flexible-OLED production; the expensive growth wafer is repolished and reused 20-50 times.
why: Delivers single-crystal, low-leakage access channels (Fact 3) at glass-panel cost; cuts substrate cost and scarce-crystal demand per bit by >10x.

title: Built-in negative-charge dielectric replaces negative wordline pumps
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight: counterbalance the depletion-mode tendency of wide-gap oxide TFTs with permanent charge. An AlOx layer on the glass substrate, carrying its native fixed negative charge (~1e12-1e13 cm-2, the effect used for solar-cell field passivation), sits under each channel as a static counterweight that shifts Vt positive by ~1 V, so the off-state is deep at a 0 V wordline.
why: Removes negative-wordline charge pumps and their periphery area and energy (Facts 7, 10) while keeping deep off-state leakage (Fact 3).

title: Sacrificial hydrogen getter keeps oxide-TFT leakage tail low for life
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: oxide-semiconductor access devices on glass drift leaky as hydrogen, a shallow donor, diffuses in from passivation and packaging. A buried Ti/Zr getter film patterned around each memory tile absorbs that hydrogen over the product life, cushioning the off-current tail before it can move.
why: Holds sub-1e-19 A leakage stable over ten years so refresh can be set in seconds (Fact 3); one cheap sputter step.

title: Millisecond flash-lamp anneal gives crystalline, low-trap stacks on cheap glass
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping (rushing through): heat only the top micrometres to ~900-1000 C for ~1 ms with xenon flash lamps, so the gate dielectric densifies and the oxide channel crystallises while the soda-lime glass or polymer substrate stays below its softening point.
why: Lower interface and bulk trap density cuts trap-assisted leakage and VRT (Fact 3) without costly quartz or sapphire substrates; flash-lamp tools are low capex (Fact 4).

title: Wafer-scale monolayer WSe2 on sapphire: junction-free atomically thin switch
idea: TRIZ #30 Flexible shells and thin films: use a 0.7 nm monolayer channel grown by MOCVD directly on c-plane sapphire and double-gated so the gate controls every atom of the channel; with no bulk, no pn junction and a ~1.6-2 eV gap, junction generation leakage vanishes and short-channel leakage stays suppressed at ~10 nm gate length.
why: A small, low-leakage access device (Facts 2, 3) on a non-silicon, crucible-free substrate; risks are contact resistance and defect-assisted leakage.

title: Modulation-doped In2O3/Ga2O3 superlattice channel resolves mobility versus leakage
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite materials: build the channel on glass as an ALD superlattice of ~1 nm In2O3 wells and Ga2O3 barriers, so electrons in the wells give high mobility when the gate fills them, while in the off state the wide-gap Ga2O3 barriers set the leakage floor and trap out oxygen-vacancy donors.
why: Breaks the drive-vs-leakage contradiction of single-composition oxides (Fact 3): target >30 cm2/Vs with <1e-20 A/um off-current, enabling 10-100 ns access on glass.

title: Thermally drawn multimaterial fibers as one-dimensional memory substrates
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: replace the 2D wafer with a 1D substrate. A macroscopic preform of chalcogenide-glass semiconductor, polymer dielectric and metal electrodes is thermally drawn into kilometres of fiber whose cross-section is one memory column (bitline, storage electrodes, access channel); fibers are then woven or laminated with orthogonal wordline fibers into 3D blocks.
why: Capital intensity (Fact 4): draw towers make kilometres per hour with no lithography, and wide-gap chalcogenides give low leakage (Fact 3); density and speed are highly speculative.

title: Laminate a hundred ultrathin glass memory sheets into a 3D block
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: instead of growing 26+ tiers monolithically, build one memory tier per 25-50 um flexible-glass sheet roll-to-roll, test every sheet, then nest 50-100 known-good sheets in a laminated stack with edge-plated wordline/bitline risers and a periphery chiplet at the edge.
why: Sidesteps the 3D DRAM tier-yield problem (Fact 2) with test-and-discard per tier; ultrathin glass is U.S.-made, and low-leakage TFTs let each tier refresh at ~1 Hz (Fact 3).

title: Wide-bandgap memory carve-out funding conversion of U.S. power-device fabs
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: government acts as the intermediary between under-used U.S. SiC/GaN power-electronics lines and hyperscaler demand. A CHIPS-style program co-funds converting 150-200 mm wide-bandgap lines into refresh-free memory pilot lines and backs them with five-year hyperscaler offtake contracts for low-refresh capacity tiers.
why: U.S. manufacturability (1-2% share) and capital intensity: reuses existing tools and cleanrooms instead of $15B greenfield fabs; non-silicon substrates avoid the Spruce Pine quartz-crucible chokepoint.

title: Backlight-powered loadless latch on glass holds bits with photocurrent
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: oxide TFTs are normally shielded from light because it raises leakage; instead deliberately bathe a transparent glass memory panel in steady dim backlight. Each cell is a cross-coupled n-type TFT pair whose high node is held up by a photodiode's photocurrent (replacing the pull-up of a loadless SRAM), tunable by light intensity to out-supply leakage at any temperature.
why: Refresh-free static storage with only n-type oxide TFTs, which lack a PMOS for normal SRAM (sidesteps Fact 3); backlight power is shared and dimmable.

title: Atmospheric mist-CVD gallium oxide access transistors on sapphire panels
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics and hydraulics: deposit corundum-phase alpha-Ga2O3 (Eg ~5.3 eV) channels from an ultrasonic aerosol of gallium acetylacetonate solution carried by gas at atmospheric pressure onto sapphire, with no vacuum tools, then pattern access transistors whose thermal generation leakage is effectively nil.
why: Ultra-wide gap gives retention far beyond 64 ms (Fact 3); atmospheric aerosol deposition slashes capital intensity (Fact 4). Gallium supply is China-concentrated, so a recycling loop is part of the plan.
